title: GlusterFS on EL10: Install It and Create Your First Replica-3 Volume
summary: A practical introduction to running GlusterFS on EL10-compatible systems, creating a three-way replicated volume, and testing the result safely.
author: Eliware
content:
# GlusterFS on EL10: Install It and Create Your First Replica-3 Volume

GlusterFS lets you build a shared filesystem from storage on multiple Linux servers. A replica-3 volume keeps a full copy of each file on three bricks, so the volume can continue serving data when one storage node is unavailable.

This guide explains the shape of a small three-node installation and the checks that matter before you trust it with real data. It is written for EL10-compatible systems and for people evaluating the Eliware GlusterFS Repository.

> This is a learning and evaluation guide. Test the exact failure, recovery, backup, and workload behavior you need before using any distributed storage system in production.

## What you will build

The finished test cluster has:

- three GlusterFS server nodes;
- one dedicated, node-local brick directory on each server;
- one replica-3 volume with one brick on each node; and
- a Linux client that mounts the volume through the native GlusterFS client.

The three copies improve availability, but replication is not a backup. It will not protect you from accidental deletion, application corruption, ransomware, or a mistake made on every copy. Keep an independent backup and recovery plan.

## Before you begin

Use three servers with:

- an EL10-compatible operating system;
- stable hostnames and addresses that resolve between all three nodes;
- dedicated storage for the brick directory;
- synchronized system time; and
- firewall rules that permit Gluster management traffic and direct brick traffic between the servers and clients.

Do not place a brick inside a directory that is already being used as a general-purpose shared mount. A brick should be a dedicated directory on storage owned by that Gluster node.

For a first test, name the nodes `gluster1`, `gluster2`, and `gluster3`, and use `/data/brick1/testvol` as the brick directory on each node. Substitute your own names and paths in the commands below.

## Install the packages

Install the GlusterFS server and client packages from the repository you have selected. The Eliware repository provides EL10-compatible RPMs and an installation path for the current published package set. Start from the [Eliware repository home page](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/) for the current instructions.

On each storage node, verify that the server and native client commands are available:

```sh
gluster --version
mount.glusterfs --version
```

The exact package names and service-management commands can vary with the distribution packaging. Follow the package instructions for your system rather than copying an install command intended for another EL10-compatible distribution.

## Prepare the brick directories

On every GlusterFS server, create the dedicated brick directory and confirm that the underlying filesystem is mounted where you expect:

```sh
sudo mkdir -p /data/brick1/testvol
df -h /data/brick1/testvol
```

Keep the brick path consistent across the nodes while you are learning. In a production design, use dedicated storage, document the filesystem and mount options, and make sure the path remains present after a reboot.

## Form the trusted storage pool

Start the Gluster management service on all three nodes, then connect the nodes from one server. The service name may be `glusterd` or a distribution-specific equivalent.

From `gluster1`, probe the other two nodes:

```sh
sudo gluster peer probe gluster2
sudo gluster peer probe gluster3
sudo gluster peer status
```

You should see both peers connected. If a probe fails, check hostname resolution, the management port, service status, and firewall rules before proceeding. A successful peer probe does not prove that client-to-brick traffic is working.

## Create and start a replica-3 volume

From one node, create the volume with one brick on each server:

```sh
sudo gluster volume create testvol replica 3 transport tcp \
  gluster1:/data/brick1/testvol \
  gluster2:/data/brick1/testvol \
  gluster3:/data/brick1/testvol
```

Start it and inspect the result:

```sh
sudo gluster volume start testvol
sudo gluster volume info testvol
sudo gluster volume status testvol
```

The volume should report three bricks and a started status. The order and placement of bricks matter: keep the replica set distributed across separate failure domains. Three directories on one server are not equivalent to three node-local bricks on three servers.

## Mount the volume from a client

Install the native GlusterFS client on a Linux client, create a mount point, and mount the volume using a Gluster server name:

```sh
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/testvol
sudo mount -t glusterfs gluster1:/testvol /mnt/testvol
```

Confirm that the mount is active and write a test file:

```sh
mountpoint /mnt/testvol
printf 'hello from GlusterFS\n' | sudo tee /mnt/testvol/hello.txt
cat /mnt/testvol/hello.txt
```

The initial server address is used for discovery. After receiving the volume configuration, the native client communicates directly with the brick processes. This means a network path that permits discovery but blocks the advertised brick ports can still produce a failed mount or unusable volume.

In the Eliware Kubernetes topology, discovery traffic and direct brick traffic are intentionally separate. The discovery endpoint must not be treated as a proxy for all brick connections.

## Test a single-node failure

A replica-3 volume should be tested under the failure you intend to survive. For this first exercise, stop GlusterFS on one node while leaving the other two available. Do this only with test data:

```sh
sudo systemctl stop glusterd
```

From the client, read the file and create another small test file:

```sh
cat /mnt/testvol/hello.txt
printf 'written while one node is offline\n' | sudo tee /mnt/testvol/during-test.txt
```

Restore the node, start its service, and inspect the volume and heal state:

```sh
sudo systemctl start glusterd
sudo gluster volume status testvol
sudo gluster volume heal testvol info
```

Recovery is a process, not a checkbox. Watch the heal output and verify the data after the previously unavailable brick returns. Also test client behavior, application timeouts, and the operational steps your own environment requires.

## The network detail that surprises people

GlusterFS uses management and brick traffic. The client first discovers the volume, then connects to the brick processes that serve it. Opening only the discovery port is insufficient.

Before troubleshooting a mount, verify:

- all peers resolve to the intended addresses;
- GlusterFS is running on every expected server;
- the discovery port is reachable;
- the configured brick-port range is reachable directly from clients;
- the server advertises addresses that clients can actually route to; and
- the brick filesystem is mounted and labeled correctly for the host security policy.

This is especially important in Kubernetes, where a Service can make discovery appear healthy while pod-to-pod or client-to-pod brick connections remain blocked.

## What replica 3 does not solve

Replica 3 is a strong starting point for a small, three-node shared filesystem, but it does not remove the need for operations:

- replication consumes roughly three times the raw data capacity before filesystem overhead;
- a degraded volume needs monitoring and healing;
- split-brain conditions require investigation and deliberate resolution;
- backups must be stored independently; and
- workloads should be benchmarked against the volume profile they actually need.

Read the official [GlusterFS architecture guide](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/Quick-Start-Guide/Architecture/) and [client setup guide](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/Administrator-Guide/Setting-Up-Clients/) alongside this tutorial. When you encounter a heal or split-brain condition, start with the official [split-brain troubleshooting guide](https://docs.gluster.org/en/main/Troubleshooting/resolving-splitbrain/).

## Where Eliware fits

Eliware publishes GlusterFS packages and runtime images for people who want a repeatable way to install and evaluate GlusterFS on current infrastructure. The accompanying operator console is designed to make cluster, volume, file, NFS-Ganesha, audit, and permission operations more visible without hiding the underlying storage model.

The project currently focuses on a three-node Kubernetes-oriented design with node-local persistent bricks, a protected shared-state volume, and separate application volumes. It is experimental, so the design and deployment instructions should be treated as a starting point for testing rather than a substitute for your own operational review.

If you are ready to try the package path, begin at the [Eliware GlusterFS Repository](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/). If you are still learning the storage model, continue with our guide to [what GlusterFS is and when to use it](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/).
